questions.question: What actually counts as 'AI slop' under YouTube's monetization policy, versus legitimate AI-assisted content?
questions.answer_summary: Coverage describes YouTube targeting 'mass-produced,' 'repetitive,' and 'inauthentic' content patterns specifically, not AI tool use itself — the policy distinguishes output characteristics from the production method.

questions.question: Are faceless YouTube channels specifically targeted, or just low-effort content in general?
questions.answer_summary: The Hollywood Reporter and The Next Web both report faceless creators being disproportionately hurt by the crackdown even when their content isn't actually 'slop,' because the policy struggles to distinguish format from intent.

questions.question: How large was the actual impact of YouTube's AI slop crackdown?
questions.answer_summary: Tech Times reported that YouTube 'wiped 35M subscribers' in connection with the AI slop crackdown, giving a concrete scale indicator.

questions.question: Are small/solo creators hit harder than large studios by the new monetization rules?
questions.answer_summary: Kotaku specifically reported small creators 'feeling the crunch' under YouTube's updated monetization rules.

questions.question: Did other platforms follow YouTube's lead on AI content crackdowns?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — Meta/Facebook and Snapchat both introduced parallel restrictions around the same period, limiting monetization or full-AI generation for creators.

questions.question: What specific tools are solo creators actually using to build an AI production pipeline end-to-end?
questions.answer_summary: Real developer-built tools spotted on Hacker News cover distinct pipeline stages: niche/CPM research (channel-analysis tool spanning 400K+ channels), script-to-video generation, AI stock footage generation, and thumbnail CTR optimization.

questions.question: Is there evidence solo creators are measuring/optimizing thumbnail performance with AI tools?
questions.answer_summary: One HN builder reported moving click-through rate from 1.2% to 2.3% for a faceless niche channel using a purpose-built AI thumbnail generator.

questions.question: Do marketers view the AI slop crackdown positively while creators are anxious about it?
questions.answer_summary: Digiday's coverage frames the split explicitly: 'creators concerned, marketers cheering.'

questions.question: Has YouTube's AI content policy been stable, or is it still being clarified?
questions.answer_summary: YouTube had to 'clarify' its AI slop policy multiple times (2025 and again in 2026) after creator confusion, indicating rules are still evolving rather than fixed.

questions.question: Despite the crackdown, is low-cost AI-generated content still earning meaningful revenue on YouTube?
questions.answer_summary: One industry piece reported that some cheaply-produced AI videos are still earning significant revenue even amid the policy changes, suggesting uneven enforcement.
